card vi-sysdiag-proto  [proto]
Prototype: fold werk's own decided set into one dependency diagram, then change one card
why: Three decided cards rest on an untested assumption — that an agent can read a set of decision cards and name the components of the product. #vi-sysdiag-derive, #vi-sysdiag-grain and #vi-sysdiag-declare are all wrong if it cannot.
subtree: 41 cards, 7 open, 8 proto, 26 decided, 4 unchallenged, 2 stale

Scope, in order. Nothing outside this list.

1. Fold the decided cards of the werk subtree into one Mermaid file, by hand, per #vi-sysdiag-format. Level 1 and level 2 only, per #vi-sysdiag-zoom.
2. Load Mermaid from a CDN and draw it in a tab beside the tree and the 3D graph.
3. Change one card. Redraw with the old file in context. Record whether the result is local or a restructure, per #vi-sysdiag-declare.

Not in scope: the data flow diagram, because #vi-flow says werk is the one project where it cannot be trusted. Not in scope: any layout code, per #vi-sysdiag-format:opt0. Not in scope: automating the fold — step 1 is done by hand, to find out what the fold needs before a command wraps it.

What it can show is false:

- the card set does not name components, only views and schema and build steps
- the same card set folds two different ways on two reads, so there is no stable diagram to be continuous with
- every one-card change reads as a restructure, which would mean the drawing carries no reusable structure

card vi-sysdiag-ask  [decided]
A missing arrow is a question for the map to ask
why: Step 1 drew 24 parts and no arrow came from a card. If the tool treats that as missing data, it fills the arrows in from the code and the gap disappears. If it treats it as an open question, the tool does the job #visual asks of it: it coaches judgement.

The tool draws the parts. Then it asks about the blank arrows.

"The chat pane and the agent runner are both parts. How do they talk?" That is a question with an answer, and the answer is a decision. So it becomes a card.

This is the first case where the diagram writes to the map, not the other way round. It fits #vi-compl: the tool does not choose the answer, it finds the missing question.

It also gives the diagram a way to be incomplete on purpose. A blank arrow is a real state, drawn as a dashed line with a mark. A tool that cannot draw "we have not decided this" will guess instead.

card vi-sysdiag-declare  [proto]
A redraw declares whether it was a local edit or a restructure
why: A whole-file redraw can move anything. Without a statement of which it did, the reader must diff the picture to find out, and a restructure looks the same as a rename. This is the one real cost of #vi-sysdiag-grain, and it is not paid by storage shape.

Two outcomes, named on the redraw:

- **local** — the same components and the same grouping, with text or one edge changed. The reader can trust their mental model.
- **restructure** — a boundary moved, a component split, or a group re-formed. The reader has to look again, and the redraw says why.

A restructure is the interesting event. It means a single card changed something that the previous reading of the whole card set had wrong. That is worth surfacing in the map, not hiding in a picture.
